Why do metal based rocks burn up in immense fires when entering our atmosphere, but metal based rockets and a tinfoil based landing module make it out of, then back into Earth's atmosphere un-phased?

It's very simple; most of the speed is gained in the upper atmosphere, and the rest is gained outside the atmosphere. Why? Because it's far more efficient to accelerate the rocket outside the atmosphere than inside it.

Then when the rocket returns, its speed relative to atmospheric density will be multiple times higher, than the speed relative to atmospheric density when going up. Now why is that? Because there are no brakes when returning.

If you'd want to have the same speed profile when coming down as going up, you'd have to have rockets burning with the same power all the way down as you had when going up. The space shuttle or other vehicles do not do this, and hence the speed profile is different when coming down.

The only exception is SpaceX, which does return its rockets without burning them up, because they turn them around and actually brake, before letting them fall back to earth. This is not the only reason they do not burn up, but it gives you an idea that there are multiple ways to bring stuff back down, while still retaining speed profiles that do not make things blow up.

But once you have put something in orbit, the speed is so high, it becomes much more difficult to reduce the speed without having a profile that makes steel melt when coming down.

So in summary: it's because of different speed profiles. Lower speed at higher air density when going up, and much higher speeds at the same or similar air density when coming down.

If you'd have vehicles that could accelerate and brake the same way when going up as coming down, you would not have this problem. Unfortunately we have not invented propulsion technology that makes this possible yet.
